\title{Duplicates Cause the Cliff, Synthetic Data the Slope: Recursive Training and Induction Circuits}

% TODO(author): replace with the real author name(s), 1--3 people.

\section{Abstract}
{
\bf
\looseness=-1
Training on model-generated data risks \emph{model collapse}, while much
in-context learning relies on \emph{induction heads}. We run 10-generation
fit$\to$sample$\to$refit pipelines on a few-shot task that only induction can
solve. Collapse first looks abrupt (51 of 72 later models fail), but duplicated
sequences and early stopping in our protocol caused it. With a fixed budget, no
duplicates and a real-data control, fully synthetic training yields no failures
from healthy starts but a slow decline (final accuracy 0.947 vs.\ 1.000,
$p{=}0.005$); half-real data removes it. Classic induction heads give way to heads
at other offsets, yet every accurate model keeps a layer-0$\to$1 key-composition
edge. A weak first generator is the real risk (one seed).
}
\begin{quote}
\small
\textbf{Keywords:} induction heads; model collapse; mechanistic interpretability
\end{quote}

\section{Introduction} \label{Intro}
\looseness=-1
Models are increasingly trained on earlier models' output.
\citet{shumailov2023curse,shumailov2024ai} show that recursively fitting
generation $n$ to samples from generation $n{-}1$ erodes the tails of the learned
distribution, measured through output statistics; the model's internals are little
studied. We study the \emph{induction head}, a previous-token head feeding a later
head that attends to what followed an earlier occurrence of the current token and
copies it \citep{olsson2022incontext}, on the few-shot task of
\citet{singh2024needs}, where per-sequence relabelling forbids memorisation. ACDC
\citep{conmy2023towards} finds circuits by patching graph edges; mechanistic data
attribution \citep{chen2026mechanistic} traces them to training data (not
implemented here). \textbf{How does recursive training change the induction
circuit, and how much of the apparent damage is real?}

\section{Methods}
\looseness=-1
\textbf{Task and model.} A sequence shows 4 of $K{=}64$ symbols, 3 times each in
random order, each with a label ($L{=}8$) drawn afresh per sequence; the target is
the query symbol's label (symbol IDs replace Omniglot). A 2-layer, 4-head, $d{=}64$
transformer trains on 20{,}000 sequences; validation and test sets (800 each) come
from the true task. \emph{Base}: loss on the query label only. \emph{Extended}:
auxiliary heads also predict the next symbol and its label, so it can generate
sequences. Hyper-parameters were compared on validation accuracy over 30
settings$\times$4 seeds; ours were within 0.01 of the best (Supp.\ Table S6).
\textbf{Pipeline.} Generation 0 trains on real data $P$; generation $n$ trains from
scratch, from the same initialisation, on
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{D}_n=\{x_i\sim q_{n-1}\}_{i\le pN}\ \cup\ \{x_i\sim P\}_{i\le (1-p)N},
\end{equation}
with $q_{n-1}$ the samples of model $n{-}1$ (the base model resamples only a real
context's label). Extended runs use $p\in\{1,0.5,0.25\}$, base $p{=}1$, 10
generations. Our first runs resampled pools with replacement (63\% distinct) and
stopped early on validation loss; the corrected runs use 150 fixed epochs, no
duplicates (except one condition), 8 seeds each with its own data, and a real-data
control ($p{=}0$). \textbf{Measures.} A model \emph{fails} below 0.5 test accuracy.
Head $(\ell,h)$'s induction score at offset $d$ is
\begin{equation}
s_d^{\ell h}=\tfrac1B\textstyle\sum_{b=1}^{B}\sum_{j\in J_b}A^{\ell h}_{q,\,2j+d},
\end{equation}
the attention from the query onto the position $d$ tokens after each earlier
occurrence $j\in J_b$ of its symbol; $d{=}1$ (the label) is the classic target,
$d{=}0$ the occurrence itself, $d{=}2$ the next symbol. A model has a \emph{classic
head} if $\max s_1\ge0.3$. ACDC runs on all 110 edges (head q/k/v inputs, MLPs,
output), cutting an edge if it raises KL(model$\|$pruned) by less than $\tau{=}0.01$,
with corrupted inputs from other random sequences or the same symbols with redrawn
labels.

\section{Results}
\looseness=-1
\textbf{The first cliff was an artifact.} In our first runs the extended model at
$p{=}1$ failed in 51 of 72 later generations. Across the two protocol choices (seeds
0--2, Supp.\ Table S2) it failed 22/27 times with early stopping and duplicates, 6/27
without early stopping, 1/27 without duplicates, 0/27 with neither; retraining first
failures without early stopping recovered 4 of 6 (Supp.\ Table S3).
\textbf{Without the artifacts there is a slope, not a cliff}
(Fig.~\ref{fig:main}b, Table~\ref{tab:main}). From the seven healthy starts, fully
synthetic training causes no failure in 63 trainings, yet final accuracy is 0.947
(minimum 0.873) against 0.9997 for real data (exact permutation test over seeds,
$p{=}0.005$); five of seven seeds end below 0.99. At $p\le0.5$ models match the
control ($p{=}0.66$, $0.27$). Duplicates at $p{=}1$ give 17/63 failures and 0.428
final accuracy ($p{=}0.004$ against no duplicates; Fig.~\ref{fig:main}a).
\textbf{A weak generator is what fails.} Seed 4's generation 0 reaches only 0.80; at
$p{=}1$ its descendants decline to 0.29, at $p\le0.5$ they swing between 0.44 and
1.00, and with real data they recover at once (one seed: a hypothesis).

\begin{figure*}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig_mech_v2.png}
  \caption{The induction circuit across generations. (a)~Median best-head score over
  the seven healthy starts: classic (offset 1) and the best of offsets 0--2.
  (b)~Share of accurate later models without a classic head. (c)~Edges in the ACDC
  circuit (label corruption, $\tau{=}0.01$) of the 459 accurate models, by their best
  head's type.}
  \label{fig:mech}
\end{figure*}

\textbf{The classic head gives way to other heads, but the composition edge stays}
(Fig.~\ref{fig:mech}). The median
classic score of the $p{=}1$ chain is 0.17--0.21 from generation 5 (control:
0.83--0.93) while every healthy-start seed keeps accuracy $\ge$0.87; the best score
over three offsets stays at 0.76--0.79. Without a classic head are 55\% of accurate
$p{=}1$ models (32/58) against 27\% under real data (17/63; Fisher $p{=}0.002$), and
all 103 such models (every condition) have a head above 0.5 at offset 0 or 2. ACDC
finds a layer-0$\to$1 key-composition edge in all 459 accurate models it analysed;
classic circuits need 10 edges (label corruption), the others 30--47, and these
models are slightly less accurate (0.989, 0.981 vs.\ 0.997). \textbf{Base failures
are not collapse:} seeds 0 and 2 fail at generations 7 and 4 on pools whose labels
are all correct, then label the next pool at chance (Supp.\ Table S5).

\section{Discussion}
\looseness=-1
Duplicates, not synthetic data as such, produce the abrupt failures; we did not test
why (plausibly they make memorising the pool easier than learning induction, and
early stopping fires during that phase). What remains is a slow erosion that
half-real data removes, in the direction of
\citet{shumailov2023curse,shumailov2024ai} but far milder, on a task whose
first-generation errors are rare. A classic score alone would have read the
migration of heads to other offsets as loss of the circuit; ACDC's composition edge
is conserved, though whether the other heads do the same job is open.
\textbf{Limitations.} (i) A symbolic task and a tiny model. (ii) One
weak-start seed. (iii) Our thresholds (0.5, 0.3, $\tau$); the non-classic circuits
are only partly understood. (iv) Tests treat seeds as independent, but trainings
within a run are not. (v) No real-data control for the base variant.

\section*{Supplementary Material}

\subsection*{S1. Setup, provenance and reproducibility}
\textbf{Configuration.} $K{=}64$, $L{=}8$, 4 exemplars $\times$ 3 repeats (12 context
pairs, sequence length 25); 2 layers $\times$ 4 heads, $d_\text{model}{=}64$,
$d_\text{ff}{=}256$; AdamW, learning rate $10^{-3}$, weight decay 0.1, batch 128, 100
warm-up steps with cosine decay, gradient clipping 1.0; 20{,}000 training sequences per
generation, 800 validation and 800 test sequences from the true distribution. Original
runs: at most 100 (base) or 80 (extended) epochs with early stopping on validation loss
(patience 40 and 30), pools resampled with replacement. Corrected runs: 150 epochs, no
early stopping, pools without duplicate sequences except in the condition marked
``dups''. Seeds set initialisation and sampling; in the corrected runs seed $s$ also
sets its own real-data pool and validation/test sets (data seed $=s$). The model
initialisation is the same in every generation of a run. A model counts as
\emph{accurate} at test accuracy $\ge$0.9 and as \emph{failed} below 0.5.

\textbf{Compute and provenance.} CPU only: mscluster Slurm nodes, 4 cores per task;
one 10-generation run takes about 1 hour. Corrected runs: job 63867 (48 runs, 6
conditions $\times$ 8 seeds). Hyper-parameter study: jobs 63405 and 63555 (cells 5 and
8 were resubmitted after a start-up race on the shared filesystem made them crash
before training). Analyses of the checkpoints: circuit scores 64119, ACDC 64130,
long-budget retraining 64133, qualitative figures 64134. Original runs: 62521
(no-collapse), 62535, 62527 and 62798 (collapse; in the first submission 6 of 9 tasks
crashed at start-up from the same kind of race and were resubmitted unchanged), then
controls 63092, extra seeds 63093 and 63094, retraining 63086, circuit and pool
analysis 63237. All 89 collapse runs completed 10 generations. Commands are in
\texttt{README.txt}; \texttt{tests/test\_pipeline.py} (end-to-end checks on tiny
configs) passed on the cluster before the corrected runs were submitted.

\textbf{Pilot observation (not part of the reported results).} With 4{,}000-sequence
pools, some initialisations memorised the training set instead of learning induction
even without collapse; 20{,}000 sequences removed this in pilot tests. Those logs were
not retained, so this only motivates the pool size.

\subsection*{S3. What was not done}
Mechanistic data attribution \citep{chen2026mechanistic} is not implemented. The
non-classic circuits are characterised by head offsets and ACDC edge counts but not
explained: how the label reaches the output in a model whose layer-1 head attends the
occurrence itself is not resolved. The base variant has no real-data control, so its
clean-data failure rate is inferred from the pools of its failures rather than measured.
Only the first failing generation of each failing run was retrained. The weak-start
finding rests on one seed.
